utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon to everybody. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm distracted by an email. Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First issue to be discussed is a follow-up to the end of yesterday's hearing. I stated that we can only decide on a day-to-day basis when really to hear a case. Just a few minutes ago, we learned that tomorrow, Courtroom I would be available not only in the afternoon but already in the morning. In the past, we discussed this question in the framework of 65 ter (i) meetings, and there was an agreement among all participants, if I may say so, that in case it's possible, we should hear the case in the morning. Are there any really absolute important objections against the suggestion to start in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence does not have any objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't objected so far, but there have been a number of changes of timing and sitting. As it so happens, we do have commitments tomorrow morning, and we would prefer - we can't obviously insist- but we would prefer that we stick to the original schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be possible to rethink this problem in the light that we should try to hear this witness during this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in addition, I think the examination by the Judges will take the entire day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a chance to discuss the matter and come back to Your Honour, or does Your Honour need a decision straight away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there's no objection by Madam Registrar, I think we can do it immediately after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's go into closed session for the next period of time. Closed and not private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Primarily we are seized with the request to hear or to admit into evidence two witnesses under Rule 92 bis, and we already heard from the Defence that they would request a cross-examination of these two witnesses in case the testimony of -- the previous testimony and the transcript would be admitted into evidence under 92 bis. We tried to assess what would be the added value of hearing these two witnesses or admitting the transcripts into evidence. And we came to the conclusion that at the end of the day, the added value would be limited - but please correct me if I'm wrong - the destruction of a mosque in Donja Ljubija. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If I'm not totally wrong, already during the 98 bis stage of these proceedings, this part of the indictment was quitted and is no longer part of our procedure. I would invite the Prosecution to instruct us what from their point of view would be the added value of the admission into evidence of these transcripts where we already, from our point of view, have certain evidence, to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we don't have the Rule 98 bis motion with us. But we understood we dropped a mosque in Donja Ravska. But that's not the point. Your Honour, we've considered the added value, as Your Honour has put it, of these two witnesses overnight, and we've taken the view that we don't wish to extend the case by the fact the Defence say they want to cross-examine, although normally, we would say that's a matter for them. And therefore, we're not seeking now to put in those two transcripts under Rule 92. So that should assist Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, you withdraw these two parts of your motion requesting the admission of transcript pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, just those two witnesses. We do maintain our request for the report of Professor Donia, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the third part of your motion, the Chamber conferred yesterday, and we reviewed our approach to this point, especially due to the fact that we are sitting now in a different composition as it was at the start of the case. You will recall that the Chamber was -- to put it very carefully or cautiously, the point of view taken by the Chamber was that in principle, history should not be subject of a judgement of a judiciary. That it's the right of each individual to have his or her own view on history, save of course it's relevant for the concrete case. And at that time, we decided that the report provided Dr. Donia would suffice to have the necessary overview about that what happened in Prijedor before and after the deplorable incidents. It is now the Prosecution's submission that we should review our point of view because Mr. Trifkovic, not in his written statement, but admittedly during his examination, he dwelled upon a number of issues which we in the light of the aforesaid would be absolutely irrelevant. But we came to the conclusion that the mere fact that a Defence expert witness discusses points of being absolutely irrelevant and, as we did it in the past, for a better flow of arguments and not to interrupt the case unnecessarily, we didn't intervene by stating this part of your testimony is irrelevant, this is not a justifying reason to review our approach taken in the beginning of this case and regarding the additional part or the more general part of Dr. Donia's report as relevant for our case and therefore, we decided to dismiss the motion for admission of expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis as rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour hear me on that for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are always open to the parties, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, the whole of Dr. Trifkovic's report as I pointed out with the exception of something like nine pages was devoted to the background and the major event, if I can put it, as opposed to Prijedor. Those were the events that Dr. Donia dealt with in his main report, and Your Honours rightly said that on the 17th of April and again on the 1st of May, when Mr. Cayley applied to put that report in, you denied the application on the basis that it wasn't specifically relevant to Prijedor. Your Honour, it is our submission that it would be unfair in the extreme even if Your Honours when you come to make a decision on the case exclude most of Dr. Trifkovic's evidence as irrelevant. It would be so unfair to have a one-sided and, we would submit, unbalanced view of the context of the events in Prijedor rather than to hear the other side. And Your Honours, we have to put it this way, even if Your Honours decide on a verdict of guilty on one or more of these charges, there is almost certain to be an appeal, equally I suppose if Your Honours decide to acquit, the Prosecution have the right to appeal and one way or another, it may be of some significance as to what evidence was led within the trial on the background to these events. And Your Honours, it's our submission that a fair trial also requires that the Prosecution have a fair hearing and a fair chance to put its evidence, particularly countering Defence evidence on specific points. So Your Honours, we do say that it is material and relevant for the main report of Dr. Donia now to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In conclusion, your point is that you ask the Trial Chamber to review the decision as of yesterday. May I ask the Defence to comment on the question of the admission into evidence of the Donia report and the question whether this would have an impact on Dr. Trifkovic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As my colleague, Mr. John Ostojic, told us on Friday, the Prosecution is actually seeking, pursuant to Rule 94, to introduce the Donia report which is from the Brdjanin/Talic case. It's not even done for our case. And we think that the Chamber have already ruled twice now correctly, because this would be actually the attempt of the Prosecution to reopen their case, not to introduce anything new. And we are in a rebuttal phase, so only if there is something new, it should be applied for rebuttal phase. The Donia report adds nothing to the charges from the fourth amended indictment. If this report is admitted, then the Defence will have to have the right to re-examine Mr. Donia again, which we think would be only unnecessarily prolong the whole procedure. We also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, the Defence is aware that the Trial Chamber has, no doubt, the right to regard in part the answers given and the statement given by Mr. Trifkovic as irrelevant for the concrete case at the end of the day when it comes down to the judgement, as it's true for the Donia report and to all other exhibits recalling our Rules on the admission of evidence that the mere admission of evidence does not mean, and I speak now about the Trifkovic report, that the mere admission into evidence does not mean that we at the end of the day come to the conclusion that an exhibit, a report, a statement or whatsoever, in its entirety, is relevant for the case. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence is aware that the Chamber has the right to apply rules to any evidence in this case, and we know that the Chamber has to give first the authenticity, weight of authenticity to that document, and then weight. So we are aware that the Chamber can admit parts of the evidence or the evidence in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have interrupted you. You wanted to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to emphasise that we think and it's our position that Donia's report is based on very limited number of documents, and that's why that report is prejudiced and not fair in regard of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in any event, your submission would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our submission would be that the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- that you would request to once again examine Dr. Donia based on his additional report prepared for Brdjanin/Talic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say this: First of all, the report doesn't touch on Dr. Stakic. That was dealt with in the Prijedor report. Second, the Defence did cross-examine on areas within that report, although the report didn't go in. And third, Your Honours, we're content if Your Honours strike out of Dr. Trifkovic's report, who I should add, never looked at a single original document. So to say that Dr. Donia's report is unfair because he only looked at some, the only pages that relate to Prijedor in the whole of Dr. Trifkovic's report are pages 23 to 25, 27 to 31 inclusive, and 36 to 37. So if Your Honours strike out the whole of the rest of the report, we're content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can the parties agree that it's finally for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Judges to assess the evidence. As there was a request to review our own position, we will come back to this after deliberation following the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that, may I ask, and I'm sorry to have to ask you, I wish to be able to speak to the Prosecutor, and the only time that she is able to see me is at 3.15. Would Your Honours kindly rise today at 3.15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now turn to exercise we are absolutely not happy with. And this is the question of the admission into evidence of exhibits tendered by the Defence at a very late stage. I take it that the Prosecution until now had no chance at all to revisit or to first -- for the first time, to have a view on documents 250 through 585?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, we have been through 250 up until 470. The remaining ones, because the bundles were being copied outside, we didn't have back until just before Your Honours sat. But we have been through the numbers up to 470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I invite you to comment on these documents. And I think this would be the first bundle, 250 to 470, and then later on document by document starting with 561. Because they are a very specific species and we have a number of questions on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm quite happy if Your Honours want to do it that way. Your Honours, can I indicate again, and perhaps we can do it this way, first of all, the ones that are already Prosecution exhibits, if I just indicate those as a group, and then actual numbers, although I can do that, can be given to -- they have already, I understand, been given to the Registry and also to Your Honours' legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be the three pages starting with 65 ter number 7 through 548. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, correct. If Your Honours already have that, there's no need for me to indicate those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, the request is moot?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We checked this, Your Honour, and the request is moot, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So therefore, let's please give this document that we don't run into even more confusion, and may I thank Ruth Karper especially for providing us with this document, do you want to tender this document for facilitating --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next available exhibit number for the Prosecution would be, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S429, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So these three pages would be Exhibit S429. And as to the fact that these documents are already admitted into evidence, all the documents mentioned there under 65 ter number of the Defence, this request is declared moot because these documents are already in evidence. So this facilitates. Then, what would be the next?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I deal then with relevance. Your Honour, if I indicate the numbers where we queried the relevance and in some cases I'll explain the problem that we have. Your Honours, as far as numbers 250 through to 255 inclusive, we can see absolutely no relevance because they are completely out of the area and appear to have no basis or connection with Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we have as a common basis, the Prosecution's motion of 3 March 2003?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Motion for leave to amend exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean the Defence motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is the list the Defence gave us last time was so illogical as to any sort of order, I've still worked off the old November list because they were at least in order there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The difficulty is that we have two sets of documents, and in fact, they are not the same documents, having the same 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, we have to rely on the latest document we received, and this is the motion by the Defence, and based on this, we have our collection of documents with us. And I think it's the only reasonable way that the latest --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- update.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents I've looked at, I have been looking at all the documents, and they bear the same numbers. So whatever -- unless Your Honours have a completely different set from the ones we were given, all the documents I looked at correspond with what's on that November the 18th list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not in all detail and not in each case. Sometimes there is a translation, sometimes there isn't. So we would prefer to work with the latest update because then we know what we are discussing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that case, I hope the list is the same. I don't see I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to continue. You stated 250 through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 250 through 255 inclusive, we query the relevance. And Your Honour, I'm dealing with them in categories now. The same with 257 and 258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, 273 to 276 are all military court judgements, and we query the relevance, first of all, because they are nearly all about desertion; and secondly, 274 to 76 all relate to desertion or failing to respond to the draft after 1992. And so that's why we query it. Document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I immediately ask, doesn't it have an impact that these documents show that there was, in fact, a military court acting at that time in Banja Luka where people could have reported to in case there is an obligation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that would be fine except as I say, 274 to 276 relate to alleged crimes in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But as to the other two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 273 is an allegation of desertion between November 1992 and sometime in 1994. So the charge was brought in 1994. But Your Honour, may I say, I don't feel terribly strongly about this, but it does seem to me there's a slight lack of relevance to documents after the period. Your Honour, 279, we query the relevance. It relates to Trebinje. 282 is another judgement of the court, but it's not the military court. It's the municipal court, and it's in 1993. 287 and 288, again, I wouldn't say we feel very strongly about it, but this is the two photographs of Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Ganic allegedly "preying" - I think they mean p-r-a-y - in front of the military troops. Again, they may or may not be doing that, but again the relevance being. 289, we query the relevance of. 423 to 427, they are all 1st Krajina Corps reports, but they are all well outside the period of the indictment. But again, Your Honour, we don't feel particularly strongly. If the Defence can show why they are relevant, we should add that there are countless documents from the 1st Krajina Corps collection in which many of which Prijedor gets a passing mention, but we don't particularly feel strongly about that. 434 is a document from 1994 with no reference back to 1992 that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can see. It's a security report on Mr. Mujadzic. And Your Honour, that's all the ones we query for relevance. I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, there's one more, 444, which is a list of persons, but it doesn't say who or what they relate to. Your Honour, the only other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would continue to include Document 470; correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I went up to 470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the other ones you can't comment yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, there's another category as such that I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are documents put forward by the Defence which start -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, can I deal with one that falls -- the part of the Islamic declaration is Document 285. Your Honour, my objection to that is the same as with the earlier books that we raised, that it's part lifted out of context. And so, Your Honour, that's a matter for Your Honour. Your Honour also asked me, while I remember, about the Halilovic book last week. I know it's on Your Honours' list, but I may as well deal with it now. Your Honour, I've checked. We don't have the whole book translated. We have in all five chapters of it translated. So I can give Your Honours the chapters if necessary, but we don't have the whole book translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the category that concerns me is a category of what's called these official notes. They start at 3 -- can I list them for Your Honour, and then I'll explain the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. But please take care about your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 312 to 314 inclusive; and 388; and then 453, 454, 456, 459, and then 461 to 3, and 465 to 70. Your Honour, these are all what's called official notes. They are the alleged records of what persons who were arrested, Muslims, allegedly said when arrested. Your Honour, the Defence have made no attempt to call any of those people whose statements were recorded. Your Honours have heard evidence of the circumstances in which these so-called interviews were conducted. My concern is this: If these documents are being put forward to show that what was said, if it was said, was the truth, then, Your Honours, we would object because clearly, we would say that if these witnesses were called by the Defence, the situation might have been very different. Your Honour, if they are put forward merely as records of what the Prijedor police supposedly recorded and what was supposedly said, that's a different matter. But it does seem to me that wouldn't help the Defence at all, and that the only reason they're putting them in is because they're going to argue that there is evidence that the people were armed, that they were formatting rebellion, that there were 3.000 people armed and ready to rise. So Your Honour, that's the objection that we have to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be the second category. We will proceed with this after the break. And the trial stays adjourned until a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Sutherland would like me to say, and I'm happy to do so, that as usual, Your Honour was quite right. We actually conceded that we had no evidence on the mosque of Donja Ljubija, and Your Honours dismissed the charges in relation to -- or the allegation in relation to Donja Ravska. I knew Donja Ravska came into it somewhere, but Your Honours were absolutely right. Your Honours, can I deal with then the question of tomorrow's sitting. I've consulted with those who it affects, and Your Honour, there's no objection from us. So if Your Honour wants to sit all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I then ask Madam Registrar to crosscheck whether all the participants in this hearing are available tomorrow morning, especially ascent by counsel in case the witness would need a lawyer, and of course interpretation and all this, and please let us know as soon as possible whether we can continue. And then we would continue the way we did in the past, from 9 to 12.30, and then from 2.00 to 4.30 in order to come through during this week with the upcoming witness. Then in the correct order, may I ask the Prosecution, what about now exhibit provisionally marked I think it was S428, the -- let's call it the statement or the guilty plea of Ms. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the situation is this: We would ask that it be marked as an exhibit for this reason: Questions were asked about the content and answers were given. But Your Honour, its only relevance at this stage would be that questions were asked on the document about the witness's knowledge of the document. At this stage, Your Honour, can I say we wouldn't be seeking for that document to have any other significance than that. But I think it has to be an exhibit, as I said before, because it has got to be something available if there is a further stage of this case where the evidence is looked at. But Your Honour, at the moment, and I stress "at the moment," Your Honour, because it's a matter of some complication as to how we deal with the actual effect of that document, I ask no more than it become an exhibit as a document that the witness was asked about and gave responses about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, to be absolutely on the safe side, it would mean that the statement as such would not be admitted into evidence, only the mere fact that there is this statement, and to that extent, we heard the witness on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can just say the mere fact that there was a statement. The content of the statement was asked about, and the witness gave certain replies. Therefore, in such a circumstance, it's our submission it needs to become an exhibit. The problem that I anticipate Your Honour has identified is how would Your Honours have to treat the content of that statement in your final judgement. At the moment, Your Honours would have to do no more than remark that the witness was asked about it and gave certain answers. But you can't have a statement without the content, if you see what I mean. But I'm not suggesting that Your Honours should use that to come to any further conclusion about or make a finding of fact as to, for example, joint criminal enterprise based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, this would be absolutely impossible based on this to come to the conclusion that you mentioned that there would have been a joint criminal enterprise. But may I hear the submission, please, from the Defence, related to this question. Would you -- could you agree that this document be admitted but only in this limited area; and in fact, not the statement as such? And I have to be quite clear on this, this would mean we have not yet discussed finally whether the result of the admission into evidence would be that at the same time, we would have that grant the right of cross-examination in case Biljana Plavsic would be available as a witness, and no doubt, this could happen during our trial. So would you be prepared to accept the admission into evidence in this limits, as pointed out beforehand by the Prosecution, and at the same time explicitly waive, if there is any, right to cross-examine Ms. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We do not agree that this document be evidence in our case, and if so, then we'll have to change our mind and to ask to cross-examine Ms. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A clear statement. And I think as to the legal difficult implications of this question, the parties will understand we can't rule immediately on this. We have to really balance the question and find the legal basis for this. Thank you for this clear answer on both sides. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Then we took the opportunity once again reviewing the question whether or not the long, put it this way, the long Donia report be admitted into evidence. And we are now absolutely clear on this issue, that we stick to that what the Trial Chamber has said already at the beginning of the case, and to the best of my recollection, also during the pre-trial phase, that for the reasons given at that time, that is, at least in April 1992 and also this afternoon, we dismiss the request finally to admit this document under Rule 94 bis. We are now in the procedural situation that I have to ask the Prosecution, is there anything else in rebuttal from the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to resist the temptation. No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the rules of logic, when there is no rebuttal, there's no rejoinder. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it remains for us to hear Mr. Kuruzovic and to go through this extremely difficult exercise on the admission of evidence. And the Office of the Prosecution, please, may not misinterpret this or misunderstand this, we complained a lot in the past about the approach taken by the Defence; but on the other hand, taking into account the limited possibilities, the limited numbers of hands-on for the Defence, I think this excuses some failures and some mistakes. And therefore, we should take this into account when we go through the documents. But I think we should continue immediately. We first heard your contribution on the documents you regard as not relevant. And the second, the official notes, being on the one-hand side not relevant or tending to start a new area of evidence not yet covered until now, especially the documents 465 through 470. Oslobodenje, date -- I can't see any date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6th of April, top right corner. Highlighted in black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. 6th of April, 1992. And you want to tender the entire page or only that what we can read on the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually only this column, this here. So it's 50 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think now the best way to proceed is to put this extremely good, legible document on the ELMO. And if you would be so kind and read extremely slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Oslobodenje, Monday, 6 April 1992. Sarajevo, year 49. Number 15732. "Bosnia and Herzegovina dramatically challenged. Hundreds of dead and wounded in Kupres, gunshots at the peace column in Sarajevo. War is raging almost in all the regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to very scarce and unverifiable information, the situation is the most difficult on the Kupres plain. "In the open conflicts, the so-called voluntary forces, Croats and Serbs, the heaviest weapons are being used. There are also indications that the air force of the army has been active in this region today. The detonations from there reach as far as Bugojno. Despite all that, nobody is absolutely certain about the real proportions of the catastrophe that is unfolding over there. Those who managed to flee at the last moment claim, according to Tanjug, that so far, there have been hundreds of dead and wounded there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The next available exhibit number, please? D120B. And the English translation can be read on today's transcript, page 57, line 14 through page 58, line 3. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Apart from the sentence "war is raging in almost all the region Bosnia-Herzegovina," it deals with Kupres and Sarajevo which is outside the Prijedor Municipality area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you don't want to continue. You want only to read the left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that it's immediately prior to the events --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the day of recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina also, the 6th of April, by some states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm aware of this, and therefore we can't automatically and at this point in time say that it's absolutely irrelevant. Therefore, admitted into evidence as D120B. 580. Once again, without any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's only text on the right-hand bottom corner. "Imminent threat of war." [Interpretation] "Imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is undisputed. And is it really necessary to introduce this once again into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because this one is issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rump Presidency, not "imminent threat of war" introduced by the Serbian Presidency, or actually Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't go into in-depth discussion of tu quoque, but you want to limit your contribution to this small article of the 9th of April Priznanja or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, actually everything else around that small box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But what is - now I have to ask the same question in your direction - the added value to what we have already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That the presidency changed the name of the state by its own, it's changed from SRB to RB. It abolished republican staff of the Territorial Defence, organised separate staff of Territorial Defence, introduced a new commander and staff of this Territorial Defence. So it's pretty detailed, has dates in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if we can proceed with this document in the same way we did it previously, and may I ask the usher to present this document, only this one, on the ELMO. This would be D121B. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D122, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: D122B. Please, and slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Imminent threat of war. This decision on the basis of the constitutional powers was taken by the presidency of BH. Instead of Socialist Republic of B and H, the Republic of B and H. RS TO, the Territorial Defence republican staff abolished, and TO staff set up. And the new commander and chief of staff appointed. "The Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina tonight proclaimed the imminent threat to war across the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina two nights ago. This decision was taken at a session of the state of leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the -- for the duration of the imminent threat of war. The Presidency of the Republic will have additional members sitting in it so that in his work will participate the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the prime minister, and the commander of the Territorial Defence. "These and other decisions were taken at a session whose work was also participated in by presidents -- by chairman of the caucuses of the Assembly of BH, the prime minister of the Republic, the Minister for People's defence. The session was not attended by Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Nikola Koljevic who notified this state body that same day that they had resigned their offices in the Presidency. "Likewise, the Presidency also decided to change the name of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to give it a new name, `The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.' A decree on the abolition Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the former republican staff of the TO was adopted encompassing also the establishment of the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among other things, this decree states that the Presidency of BH will decide on the employment of units of the TO of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the Ministry for the People's Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through the TO staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, will run and command the TO forces. "The decree likewise says that the provisional, official insignia of all members of the TO is the ancient Bosnian coat of arms in the form of a shield, blue, with a white bar crossing it diagonally and with three golden yellow lilies in each of the fields. In the same decree of the Presidency, it is dismissed the former commander of the republican staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Lieutenant-General Drago Vukosavljevic, and the chief of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Lieutenant-General Fikret Jahic. And appointed pointed Colonel Hasan Efendic the commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Colonel Stjepan Siber, the chief of staff of the Territorial Defence. This decree entered force two nights ago. "The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took all those decisions pursuant to constitutional powers, pursuant to its constitutional powers, because two mornings ago, the chairman of the caucuses in the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had informed the members of the Presidency that the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which has been sitting for the past three days without interruption, was unable to adopt the necessary legal acts because in the newly emerged political situation, because of the absence of quorum. And this situation, the Presidency, has termed the imminent threat of war. "The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall continue to use its constitutional powers to pass the necessary decisions and decrees, and when the necessary conditions are provided, that is, when a sufficient number of members of parliament of the republic attend this session (121 members of parliament), the Assembly shall inform the state leadership that it will continue to perform its constitutional obligations and tasks. "In adopting these decisions and the decrees, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina concluded two nights ago -- at its session two nights ago that the legality and the legitimacy of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian parliament should not be suspended and called upon the members of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina to gather in Sarajevo. "It was said that if some members of parliament were fighting on the front, then it would be better if they engaged in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the parliament where they had been elected as representatives of peoples, that is, their municipalities. "The Presidency of B and H, on behalf of the members of the parliament who participated in the work of this body of the state, the chairman of the caucus of the MBO, the Muslim/Bosnian organisation, Dr. Muhamed Filipovic, transmitted the requests of the members of parliament in Sarajevo which addressed the following issue: The Assembly of B and H should be in permanent session. Then the international public opinion should be kept abreast with the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the JNA should recognise the supreme civilian authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to request from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to adopt the law on the establishment of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was also requested to adopt a law on the invalidation of all federal laws which are in contravention with the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to pass new laws which would be -- which would reflect the spirit of that recognition."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Signed by R. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This article would be in fact D121B. And the transcript reflects the English interpretation from page 59, line 24, through page 63, line 3. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under this number. With the next two articles, based on my own perusal, I have some problems as to the relevance. May we start with 582; apparently it's referring to some events --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tuzla, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Beside the attack on the army in Sarajevo in Dobrovoljacka Street, one of the biggest massacres before the events in Prijedor is the massacre of the JNA soldiers in Tuzla. And it had a profound effect on the whole Bosnia-Herzegovinian community. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think counsel is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would call it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Leading evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I could call it argument, and we are grateful that Defence counsel is prepared to read this evidence. But in fact, we have to limit ourselves to the necessary, and it's undisputed that there was a period of war, otherwise some prerequisites of the charges of the Prosecution would not be established. And therefore, I think it's not disputed that similar heinous crimes were committed also in other areas and by other ethnicities in former Yugoslavia. So therefore, we can't the relevance especially of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, even Judge Vassylenko asked our expert military expert witness, did he believe that Muslims in Prijedor area attacked military aiming to gain victory against military columns? We can see in that period of time, exactly 16th of May, attack on military column on which Muslims won. They killed or captured every single soldier in this column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Tuzla. In Kozarac, they tried unsuccessfully. But there was attempt similar or the same to this one, few days after this successful operation of Bosnian TO. Only eight days after this incident, the attack on military convoy took place in Kozarac. So we think that it shows clearly that there was order from one place, that all military convoys should be attacked, military installations should be attacked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please refrain from arguing. I think we have got your point. Submission by the Prosecution as to the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been no translation read out. I don't know what it says, apart from Mr. Lukic's assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then we have to, unfortunately, to proceed in the same manner. May I ask you, then, we stay in the same order, the first following article would be 581, once again not translated. But I take it that you want only these three columns on page 2. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the relevance would be, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is another attack on a military convoy in Sarajevo, I just mentioned. It's conducted on the 4th of May, 1992. And then in that military convoy, soldiers were also slaughtered, not as many as in Tuzla, but the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's undisputed. Mr. Lukic, can we compromise that we admit into evidence 582, because, in fact, it's closer to the incidents you just mentioned. Can we proceed this way, that we limit ourselves to 582?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both of them come after the issued order by Alija Delimustafic for which the Prosecution said it has actually never took place. So we think that both of these incidents show that this decision has been issued and that according to that decision, all these attacks were performed. So although I know that it's maybe, Your Honour, enough for you to have only one of these paper clips, we think that it's necessary to have both of them. We could offer many more regarding this, but we already choose only those two because they were the most -- well, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the most well-known ones, so that's why we choose two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in the moment, we have to take a pragmatic approach and, please, put it on the ELMO and please read it out slowly. This would be now really D122B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Oslobodenje, Monday, 4th May, 1992. Truth with new threats. Alija Izetbegovic released only in the evening from the military prison. Drama surrounding the evacuation of the military command of the 2nd Army District. General Kukanjac claims that his convoy was subject to a crime in Dobrovoljacka Street. Foreign observers cannot confirm allegations about victims. General Djurdjevac announces the threatening movements of 12.000 people from Romanija towards Sarajevo. Will the announced talks take place today? The talks between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the JNA? "The terrorist military abduction of the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina which astonished the world on Saturday evening came to an end on Sunday evening after almost 24 hours. Within the frame of the agreement which envisaged the safe evacuation of the command of the 2nd Military District from Sarajevo, Alija Izetbegovic returned to his office in the Presidency. But this was just an introduction into a new drama; namely, the army accused Bosnia-Herzegovinian authorities that despite the achieved agreement, the safe evacuation of the military convoy from the town has not been secured. "My men were subject to a crime in Dobrovoljacka Street in Skenderija. Over one half of the convoy has been cut off and came under attack. There are dead and wounded there. Twenty-five lorries have been confiscated, stated the commander of the 2nd military district, General Mile Kukanjac. General McKenzie confirmed there were problems with the convoy. He is from the UNPROFOR command, and he was one of the escorts of the convoy. However, foreign observers could not confirm the statements on the losses suffered by the convoy, and the European envoy, Major Colin Doyle says that the allegation about 25 confiscated lorries is an exaggeration. He also states that he has been informed about the confiscation of nine lorries, and he says that he would be disappointed if the agreement on the safe evacuation of the command has been violated. This would raise the following question: Do the Presidency and the Territorial Defence staff actually control their armed forces, stated Doyle. The problems with the convoy, even before General Kukanjac spoke to the military circles, have been used for a new threat against the general population of Sarajevo. General Vojislav Djurdjevac stated that 12.000 men-strong forces are moving towards the city, and he said: `I cannot stop these men'. "This was nothing else but a new confirmation for a high military position that the truce is being abused again, not only by the new attacks of the Chetnik terrorist forces on Sarajevo, which shelled the town and tried to penetrate into certain parts of the city throughout the duration of the negotiations, but also that the truce is being used for the regrouping of the aggressor forces, for bringing in new units, and for taking positions for the attack on town." That's the part we want to introduce. And if you want, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's quite clearly reflected what you want to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber. This would be D122B. And the English translation is reflected on today's transcript, page 66, line 1 through page 67, line 18. And let's immediately proceed with the Planula i Tuzla. That would be D123B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Oslobodenje" -- [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpretation is frozen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was "Oslobodenje, Saturday, 16th of May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As the army column passed through the town, Tuzla is ablaze. Five army vehicles loaded with ammunitions, weapons, and shells set on fire causing a major fire. Tuzla authorities claim that the former JNA is responsible for the incident. Tuzla, May 15th. A more trivial yet worse incident between the former JNA and the Territorial Defence and the MUP in Tuzla could not have happened. Tonight around -- last night around 1900, at the crossroads in Brcanska Malta where the streets from the direction of the Husinska Buna barracks intersects with Slavinovici and the centre of the town, five army vehicles loaded with ammunition, weapons, and shells were set on fire. "The incident started with the hell-like bursts of fire from firearms. Selim Beslagic, the mayor of Tuzla, immediately communicated on the local television, FS3, that the fire from the convoy was opened by -- first by the soldiers who were happy that they were leaving town. The Territorial Defence and the police responded. "The detonations and explosions of ammunition crates went on for two hours beneath the windows of skyscrapers. Several flats burnt down as well. So far, it has been communicated that four soldiers and one child were wounded and rescued. The smoke was billowing and going as far as 50 metres up. All this was transmitted live by the local television whose studio is 300 metres away from the fire. "Only a few hours after the press conference at which good news about the negotiations between the municipal authorities and the command of the Husinska Buna barracks, today an incident took place in Tuzla once again at Brcanska Malta with a military APC which left the barracks. It was communicated that the army had tried to take the TO weapons from Tuzla. The convoy was returned to the barracks before the eyes of the Tuzlans who watched it all on their screens. Three hours later, a convoy left the area once again, and once again it carried weapons and ammunition. The members of the TO and MUP stopped the convoy again, and then hellish gunfire started. "It was reported that there were more wounded on the road towards Slavinovici, and that the members of the TO and the army had clashed there. It was late into the night -- it is late, and it is uncertain how all this would end up in Tuzla and will it escalate into a major conflict? The Tuzla authorities call up on the army to calm down the atmosphere and to start talks. At this moment, thousands of Tuzlans are in shelters. Columns of military vehicles cannot pass through the town tonight. Firemen in neighbouring communities and companies are called upon to hurry to the rescue. Some have already arrived and are putting out the fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for this assistance. This would be D123, or 4, Madam Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 123, Your Honour.

utterances.text: We discussed this in the meantime, and we believe there might be some relevance in these documents, and therefore, we decided to admit these documents into evidence under the respective exhibit numbers. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.text: So you withdraw 585. utterances.text: That's the only document we found related -- actually we received related to the appointment of Mr. Drljaca. We asked for 1992, and this is what we got.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, is Mr. Lukic talking about 1992 or this 1994 document? I don't know what it says, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a document on the appointment, because it was not possible to get any documents on 1992. Therefore, in the moment, I can't see any relevance of the document of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.text: And the role of Simo Drljaca, I think it has been highlighted by numerous exhibits and witness testimonies and I don't see that it's in dispute that he was appointed.

utterances.text: The Prosecution claims that he was appointed by the Municipal Assembly. So we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were informed that they don't have anything from 1992, whether it's burned or ...

utterances.text: Maybe this could be replaced by a law, and we did not introduce any laws regarding interior affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 585, I understood you already withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before my learned friend expresses, but 583 is the document regarding 1992. It's military -- from the military, and it's for 1991 and 1992, only Simo Drljaca is for 1994.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document behind 583 is dated the 15th of February 2000, and I don't see any --

utterances.text: In the text --

utterances.text: The Prosecution would say it's not relevant to the indictment. It's a 1994 document.

utterances.text: After deliberations, dismissed as not relevant. This is 584. 585 is already withdrawn. So the final document we have before us, for all participants, it is the now remaining document, 583. This concludes, then, today's hearing, if you could please be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, Banja Luka. Number 8/1-08-77-2/02. Date, 15 February 2002. "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Justice. Office for Communication with the International Tribunal in The Hague. "Regarding your enactment number 02/1-773-31/02. "With regard to your request by the enactment of the general staff of the army Republika Srpska, internal number 03/2-155-2, dated 12th February, 2002, we hereby inform you on the following, and we quote: "We hereby inform you that the appointment of military commanders and their deputies in military units who were stationed in Prijedor Municipality during the period between 1991 and 1992 was dealt with according to the line of command in the army. "It transpires from the aforementioned that Mr. Milomir Stakic, as the president of the Municipal Assembly and the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor, in the aforementioned period, could not have any influence on the election and appointment of military commanders and their deputies. "Liaison officer, Zoran Cvetkovic." And the seal bears the following words: "Republika Srpska." The number on the seal, 1. The last line on the seal, illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document signed by a liaison officer purporting to know what was going on in Prijedor in 1992. We don't know what it's based on, what documents he has come to this decision in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rule on this document as soon as possible and as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore we have to carefully review this document before we come to a final conclusion. So this completes the attempt to go through these documents, from 561 until 585. Are there any other issues to be discussed urgently today?

utterances.text: There's no other issues. Only when necessary, I can comment every single disputed document by the Prosecution, and I think that I already have some notes if Your Honours are interested to hear those arguments. I'd like to provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
